projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Eleanor D. Weil was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the World War II oral history of Elenore D. Weil. Mrs. Weil was on the home-front in America and worked in a defense factory. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mrs. Weils's home in Mentor, Ohio on February 7th, 2003. Mrs. Weil was 78 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I was living in Melrose, Massachusetts, which is a suburb of Boston, something like -- is to Cleveland. And '41, good grief; yes, I was just going to college then, Massachusetts College of Art. And I remember my dad was an air-raid warden.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In Massachusetts?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: In Melrose.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Melrose was about 7 miles from the ocean and they said the U-boats were out there and we had black-out curtains and all that stuff. And practically his --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did anybody spot any U-boats out there?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: If they did they didn't tell us. I think they would have panicked if we had thought they were out. But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kind of things would your dad do as air-raid warden?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, he had the helmet and the lipstick and the full bit and he would practice going out and pretending, bodies and all that sort of thing. And he would -- we never had the actual thing, but we had to be alert and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. The lipstick, what was that for?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: That was to mark the forehead or a body or --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now what would they mark on the forehead?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, I'm not sure what he would. I don't remember. Whether it was just a cross if he was dead and then pick up immediately if he was not or something. I really don't know. I don't remember that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But that was part of his regular --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: That was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Marking --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: -- what he learned. And he had a route that he walked when -- a lot of people in the neighborhood did and they all had different routes. And it was kind of a little club actually.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now was he an air-raid warden after the war began for America?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So tell us, take us back a little bit, do you remember December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me as much as you can from that day.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, my goodness. I say I remember it I may have -- I remember -- well, that was in the European war?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No. That was the, that would be the day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor, December 7th.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Okay. When did, did we go into Europe?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, that was when it pretty much all began.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You're thinking of, you're thinking of D-Day.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Yeah, because that --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's a little later, 1944.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: That's later. Yeah. Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember getting the news of the Japanese attack?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I remember I was running downstairs and saying, "Dad, they bombed Pearl Harbor. Where's Pearl Harbor?" And he seemed to know. I don't know how he knew but he did. And we all sat glued to the radio for the next week and-a-half I guess. I remember being in college -- in high school, and they called us all down to the auditorium and listened to Roosevelt's speech. And then they, what I remember is they revised our gym schedules and everybody took gym and we practiced running. We ran miles. We jumped walls, plywood walls and jumped, and all the stuff that we might need if we were attacked. That impressed me. I think I worked very hard at that. And of course everybody's brothers and so forth were running off to war but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what other things did you do in preparation for the possible invasion?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, I think when Eric called you, what Eric called you about was that I worked in a -- it had been a curtain factory, Moltens Curtain Factory; Lord, I'm dredging here. And they turned it into a small-time defense place where I made the ear padding that went around aviator's helmets. Back then they had those ear things. And there was some lady or two made stitching what we called the doughnuts, and then we filled them with kapok, with a dowel and stuffed them in. There was no air-conditioning in those days and that pile of kapok was bad. And I said well, if we had a whole generation of deaf pilots it was my fault probably. But worked like the dickens. And it was so hot and it was terrible. And when I came home my hands would be swollen. And my mom had a fit. She said, "You'll never be an artist if you ruin your hands now." So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did the kapok smell or what was bad about the kapok?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, do you know what kapok is? It's just a fiber.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Like cotton, only it's a courser thing. And it stuck to you and it, you know, we were always breathing it and -- oh, it was awful but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you start that job, was that in --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I worked all one summer. Yeah, probably a summer after it started.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you graduated from high school in '42 then or --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: '43 I think it was. I graduated high school in '38 I believe.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were still in college?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: So I was in college, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What other things did you do for the war effort, scrapped rugs, rationing, what?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, rationing, all that stuff. I remember we didn't have much to eat. That sounds terrible, doesn't it? But, you know, very little meat. Mixing up the oleo with the color so it looked like butter. And our clothes, shoes were rationed. Went to the USO every Sunday afternoon, that was my sacrifice, dance, and the sailors all came in on Sundays so we enjoyed the sailors. I don't know. It was very little gas. We did an awful lot of walking and biking and all that sort of thing but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How much gas could you get per week?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, I have no clue. I don't remember at all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'm just curious. I'm sure that's in book somewhere.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: It's got to be in a book somewhere. But I think my dad, he always used to drive me to Boston because he was working for York Machinery, York Ice Refrigeration. And so he got what, mostly what gas we got. I guess mom got the car one day a week and had to do everything at one time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there much complaining about the rationing and shortages?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, everybody complained, sure, but that was the thing to do, you know. There wasn't, there wasn't a lot of meat. What did we miss the most? Fresh fruit, I think. Fruit didn't come in very much. But of course Boston was on the Boston Harbor and I guess the ship, the fishing boats went out so we could get fish. But I can't think of --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now in those early days after Pearl Harbor when the news started coming in about the fleet being destroyed and that sort of thing was there any fear that this might turn out badly?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Uh-huh. Definitely. And not just that they might bomb Boston, because it was a major taking-off point for the navy and all that sort of thing, but everybody's sons and brothers and so forth were getting killed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did any of your classmates drop out of school and sign up?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Yeah, sometime. I can't think of the names now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have a boyfriend at that time?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: That's another thing, we were in college and all the guys were in the army or the navy or something. I think we had four apps in our college class so it was just swell.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was wrong with the four apps?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: They were hopeless and ugly.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't think you got out of the service for being ugly.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: No? Well, they were physically unadept let's say.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They had problems?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: They had problems, yeah, asthmas and all that sort of thing. Well, that was one reason we went to the USO on Sundays because we got to see some great guys.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was that like going to the USO's and dancing with those guys?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: It was just a big fun, a big ball. And then we had dinner, they served a dinner for us and them. And I don't remember that we were allowed to date them, at least not that they knew, but it was fun and I think they had fun too because it was a release.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All branches of the service there for USO?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Mostly navy at this one because it was right in downtown, it was in Cambridge, downtown Boston so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did it seem like the guys were scared about what they were up against or --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, I don't think they admitted it. You know, guys don't admit that. They're, they're going to shoot the world. I don't remember that particularly. Maybe I'm just not remembering it but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And of course the old song, "You Can't Say No To A Soldier." Did any of them ask you?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I went with a fellow who was later killed in the South Pacific but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me as much as you can about that, about him.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, he came. He was in the navy. He came -- I don't know how frequently but when his ship came in he was at the USO and we corresponded for months. And then he went to the South Pacific and that was it. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How was he killed?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, he was on a ship that went down. Actually I don't know too much about it. He was from Pennsylvania so I never met his folks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did you get the news about that? I assume that --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Through the USO, I think that was how it happened. But it was happening all the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kind of things would you write to him?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Silly things, like what I was doing in college you know, and complaining that he wasn't there, complaining about the food we had to eat and so forth. I mean it was just foo-foo kind of stuff. He couldn't tell me anything he was doing and I was just trying to take his mind off what he was doing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were his letters heavily censured or were they just short?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Short. Short.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Fine.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: He knew better than to try and do what he shouldn't do. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how long were you dating before he was killed?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, he wasn't in town very much so we, over a period of several months we got to know each other a little bit but, you know, you didn't really because it was such a, such a hard time and it was not a happy time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How much war news would you get, actual war news about what was really going on out there?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Who knew? We got what they wanted to tell us. Of course it was always on the radio and on the -- we didn't have T.V. back then. The newspapers of course.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you feel like the reports you were getting were pretty upbeat that we were making progress?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is there any point though that you, you felt like or that there was an overall feeling that there was a turning point and that we were definitely going to win this war?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I guess we hoped Normandy would do it but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were there a lot of rumors flying around before the D-Day Invasion, people speculating about when it was going to happen, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I don't think we knew much about it, at least I didn't. Maybe some people did, but it wasn't, you know, that -- what is that? "A slip of the lips sinks a ship," that was on everything, so people who did know didn't talk, but you weren't supposed to.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there any reported sabotage or anything, any spy activity going on in your area?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I remember a bunch of us girls went town to Cape Cod one time. Boy, I'm dredging this. We stayed in -- one of the gal's parents had a cottage on the Cape on the shore, right on the shore. And I remember one night we were scared out of our wits, we looked out and we could see a light flashing obviously from a small boat, it wasn't a big boat. And then we heard somebody under the porch of the cottage we were in, and I don't remember what happened after that. But we decided we might be fighting the war right there in our own beach. Silly, I don't know. But that was -- no I don't think there was sabotage right in Boston Harbor; is that what you mean?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right, or in that area, or that you heard any reports of, well - - that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, I'm sure there was but, you know, I wasn't --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you never found out if there was a submarine out there?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Never found out. No, I don't think -- I think if it was anything it was a small boat that came in from who knows where, but, you know, our imagination's really ran wild.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What do you remember of June 6th, D-Day, hearing the news about that?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: About Normandy?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Being totally shocked. Of course at that time I didn't even know, you didn't know who was, if anybody you knew was in it because they weren't releasing any information. But, well, it was bloody horrible. Any news you got was the Germans were shooting us as fast as we were getting on the beach so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is that what the early reports were was that it was pretty bleak?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, terrible. Uh-huh. And I know -- well, afterwards I learned that Herb was there, but he never talked about it. And in fact he didn't talk about the war end of it at all. When he got up to Paris -- Tomasema.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Looked exactly like our kid.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: There's a lot of that floating around. When he got up to Paris, he got out of the med corps got into, he was a musician, and he became the arranger for the 468 Army Band, whatever it was, then he had a ball. That he talked about. But he never talked about blood and guts part of it. It's funny, some guys who go through that can't not talk about it. They talk about it all the time. But him, he didn't do that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And he was in a combat outfit before that, before he got assigned to the band?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Yeah, he was a medical.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: A med.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In fact, I found a lot of these guys who didn't talk about it are talking about it now in their late seventies or eighties?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Yeah. It's easier now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I guess so.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Yeah. And then after the war, well, I met him on a blind date and after we were married we went over to Switzerland. He wanted me to see where he took all his R & R, and it was in Switzerland. And we went to Germany, part of Germany, France, we did France pretty well, and Switzerland, we skied, and it was, it was fun then.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now I've heard that after D-Day toward the end of '44 we were making progress, everybody thought it would be over around Christmas of '44, is that what you thought?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I don't remember what I thought.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You don't remember specifically about that?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No. Do you have memories of the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Only what I heard from the guys, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What were the news reports that you were hearing on that?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Bloody.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, it was terrible. It wasn't very much good until we took Paris I think, as far as I know, and I could be forgetting everything.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now the news reports you were getting, were they fairly graphic or were they upbeat?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: You must have this from guys who were there that knew better than I would.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'm talking about what you would hear over here. Did you think you were hearing propaganda or did you think you were getting a good picture of what was happening?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I guess we thought we were getting as truthful as they could be.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Without revealing --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: We'd go to the movies and see the -- what was that called? The March of --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: News reels, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: The new reels, right, the March of Time, whatever it was called and -- but I really, you know, I was doing my thing with the ear.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long did you work at that job?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, I don't know, just that summer I think. I don't think I worked more than three or four months. I just remember the heat more than anything, terrible. I don't think I'm a very good one to talk to about the war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, no, I'm getting to see it on this side. I got the overseas side of it. I'm curious to see how much information you got back here. Back then we weren't so sensitized to getting propaganda and that sort of thing, we just thought it was the truth.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, I think I so. And of course the -- there was no T.V. and the, you know, you knew Bill Malden and you knew Ernie Pile and all the names that were making a name for themselves but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now do you remember reading Ernie Pile's stories?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Good?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. I remember Bill Malden's cartoons. They made a light touch out of it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news about when FDR died?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Shock, being very surprised. And, you know, we didn't even know he was crippled, he hid that. So we -- Eleanor was doing the legwork for him but we just thought he had to stay in Washington; this is as I'm remembering it. But he could fake standing up and moving. Oh hush.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there fear that you could sense around the home-front about what would happen now that the leader was gone?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you know much about Truman?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: As I remember nothing good. He was a cocky little son of a gun. And I don't think anybody knew anything about him. Turned out he was a whole bunch better than they thought he was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So since they knew nothing there was no fear about his ability to lead you don't think?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I don't remember. Show me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Show me.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: That was probably what the whole thing was, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember V.E. Day then, which would be in May of '45?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: No. I remember V.J. Day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You remember V.J. Day. All right. Tell me about that, about celebrations or whatever from V.J. Day.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I was working at a resort up in New Hamshire and it came over at dinnertime, as I'm remembering it, and I'll tell you, in about 20 minutes everybody was wearing lampshades and standing, standing on the tables. That was a wild night. But V.E. Day, that doesn't ring any bells at all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They're weren't necessarily any big celebrations?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, there may have been but I was not involved. I was -- just relief I guess.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How about hearing the news about dropping the atomic bomb before V.J. Day, could you comprehend what that was?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Yes, that it was a turning point. But, you know, before that, at least I didn't know that they were making any such thing, or what they were really doing, I don't know that anybody outside the Washington knew, but yes, I remember when they dropped that bomb. Nobody could -- it was beyond our comprehension, I guess this is why I'm foggy because maybe by this time we figured they weren't telling us very much because we had no --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what were the reports that you heard, did they say a city in Japan was destroyed by a bomb?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Something like that. Something like that. And so many millions killed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And they said it was one bomb, or did you, I mean --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'm trying to figure out how they reported that. They said the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: They were saying, "What's an atomic bomb?"

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So they were trying to comprehend what this could be?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I think it was beyond our comprehension, the destruction, the deaths and everything. It was just -- there had never been anything like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now in the, what would it have been, a couple days in between, the two atomic bombs --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- was there a feeling that the Japanese, that nothing had changed, that the Japanese wouldn't give up?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, we we're so shocked over what they did to Pearl Harbor that I guess we were just hoping they'd kill them all because of what they did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When the second bomb was dropped it was --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Good. Keep it up. That's terrible. That's a natural reaction.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: But I don't remember if I've got those newspapers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else? I'm going to get the list of questions and see if there's anything else.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything else about that time?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that during the war years, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I remember when I was in, I was in art school -- this is crazy, I haven't thought about that until now -- they put on a parade when the guys came back from Battan. Well, they couldn't find enough people, nurses and all that sort of thing to -- we had these army trucks, and I got all duded up I -- in an army uniform, nurse's, and I remember going down Freemont Street, and that truck and women on the side saying oh, imagine what they've been through, and I never felt so terrible in all my life because it was all a lie, you know. I remember thinking oh, how could I do this? But they wanted the affect of people coming back from the war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were out there marching as if you were a survivor?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I was riding in the back of this big army truck. It was easy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They didn't have enough survivors for that or were they just letting --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, they weren't back yet or something, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The parade was scheduled?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: They just didn't come in, you know, and they turned them loose on the streets.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, boy. That was the first time, let's see what we find here. You've probably answered all these questions.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I probably answered whatever I could. It was a naive time as far as I was concerned.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, here we go: Why did you choose that activity as far as your wartime work, with stuffing?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, it was close. And I felt pride in what I was doing. I was doing something for our boys, and I didn't ever feel I could be Rosy the Riveter because I wanted to go back to college. But it was a bad summer as far as comfort and all that was concerned, but it made me feel good that I did it. I knitted all kinds of vests and sweaters and everything, all that khaki yarn.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: These were things that were said to the soldiers or through Red Cross or whatever?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that an organized thing or just something you decided to do?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I think you could go to any Red Cross and get the yarn and then take it back when you had done it; that's foggy too. You know, I'm pushing 80, I don't remember all these things.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was the first time; what kind of training were you given for your job?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Training?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was the question.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I remember some guy in charge that marched around like Hitler I guess and demonstrated -- I don't know where he came from -- how we should do it. We were paid by the piece. And we better do a good fast job because these guys needed them. I remember mostly just the kapok flying, I come home, and it's all in my hair and my clothes, and my mother would have a fit. And your hands would sweat and it would stick to them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your title?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: No title. Slave.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: War slave of labor?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Yeah, that's it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't know why they would ask this, but who was your supervisor?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I have no clue.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's what I thought.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: He went out of my mind as fast as possible I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you -- well, you already told what you disliked and like about the war. What special rules or conventions did you have to follow? If you can't answer these this just proves why I don't use this, so that's fine.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I don't remember any rules. You know, there was a whole gang sitting around these big tables with big piles of kapok all around them and we were all doing the same thing. And over here was a sewing machine and they were making the donuts for us to stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was it all women doing this?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh. Not even women, young girls. You know, I wonder what I got paid for that? 20 cents an hour probably.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you unionized?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I didn't think so. Did you develop friendships during the activity itself?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: For the time being. There were some ladies there that were not all, we weren't all young girls but there was a bunch of us high school girls and I knew them from high school. It wasn't my college people, it was people from Melrose that were there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it wasn't like lasting friendships came out of that work?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: No, I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Bonded together stuffing kapok?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Down boy. No, college was more important at that time to me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now this is a really weird question I'm going to ask: How did you feel about the war?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Let's see; how many days have I got to do this? No, I, I don't know how to even suggest saying it. Shock that my friends were going out and getting killed, shock that all these terrible things were happening. And of course eventually you do figure, well, if they say 50,000 died it's probably 100,000. We always listened to the news at night, read the papers. What did you ask me?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You've answered it.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were there any antiwar activists at that time?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I don't think so. I don't remember anyone against it. You mean like now?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, exactly. I know there were very -- obviously before we got into World War II there was a stay out movement. After we got involved if there were any left and that sort of thing so --

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you live with family, friends, or coworkers?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: My family.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: See, this is, why I've never opened this book. In what ways did the war change your activities or habits?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, the summer I worked of course everything changed. My eating habits changed just because we couldn't get the food. But I continued going to college and I went into Boston. We didn't drive in, never had a car when I was a kid, we couldn't I mean during that period. I used to walk a half a mile to the railroad station, take the train into the Miller Station in Boston, get an elevated train to Park Square; isn't this fascinating? Aren't you glad I was there?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Come up someplace, I can't remember where we come up. Then I hopped on a bus and went out to the other side of Boston and then went to the school. All of this carrying big portfolios and big boxes of paint and all this other thing. It was not an easy trip.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You talked about your eating habits changed. Did that, was that a permanent change or when the war was over did you get back to what you had done before?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Got back to good red meat. No, you ate whatever came in. Mom had her favorite grocer and when he would -- and she always bought from him to the point where he would call and tell her, hey, he's got some hamburger today if she wants it. And we'd go on down. He was within a half a mile of the house so it was one of those local shops. You couldn't buy cheese. I remember I kept a pair of rationed shoes. I threw them away, not too long ago actually. I don't know just as a momento I guess. I thought this was ridiculous. But you couldn't buy, couldn't buy stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did you basically have one pair of shoes for months and months?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, the ones I just threw away were heels but I had sneakers and, you know, everyday stuff. Cigarettes, "Lucky Strike Green Went to War," and they changed the color of the package and everybody was fighting to get hold of the cigarettes. I smoked back then. Nineteen cents a pack I think they were. We were shocked when they went up to 19 cents a pack. We couldn't buy good -- now this is my school stuff -- I don't think the paper we got to work with was as great as it should have been. The brushes certainly weren't because the bristles were not available.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's see; we know you weren't married so you can't talk about your wedding?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: This is true.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, my, I didn't think I'd have this many questions. I asked you that. What effect did the war have on your physical and mental health or that of others you knew?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, I mentioned that we, in gym, in school, we all went through hard labor.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Did a lot of running and jumping and climbing ropes and climbing walls and all that sort of thing. What else do you mean?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It said mental health so I guess, you know, hearing everything, you know, do you think that had a lasting effect on you?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I don't think. I think I was young enough that I, I think maybe when the next war came around I thought, oh, my gosh, we're going to go through this again. But I went away and worked at that resort, you know, in the summer. We had a good time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have worthwhile experiences because of the war?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I can't think of a single one right now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You did your part?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I did my part, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, this might be close to what I already asked you but what was your most memorable experience? You're allowed to pass on any of these.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is one I've never asked.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: The parade.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: That would be V.J. Day night.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've certainly never asked this question and I'm curious to hear the answer: Most memorable character?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Am I going to malign somebody now?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I guess, unless there's some wild, wacky character there at the plant.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: No. No. I think that's for the guys in the army.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, these are the civilian questions.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Believe it or not. There's two sets of questions. I think I might be reading from the right list. I hope so.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, my goodness.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Most humerus experience?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: V.J. I guess.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Have you visited any memorials or participated in any commemorations of the war?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, I visited the -- I've been to Hawaii and I went to the one that sunk there, what was that, years ago?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The Arizona?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: The Arizona. Uh-huh. And we went on that. I've been all over the world. If it's been memorialized I've been through them if they were there but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now you mentioned the rationing and that sort of thing; was there much of a black market think going on there with people trying to buy on the sly?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, I'm sure there was. I'm sure there was but I didn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: That wasn't a personal experience. As far as I was concerned I wasn't earning any money anyway, I couldn't by a whole lot.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've already asked you some of these questions.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Good. See, you're smarter than you thought you were.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, I guess this is probably a good one: Was there a lack of social opportunities and friends because of the war?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, heck yes, no men.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I guess you did answer that one. Those ugly four guys?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, probably, like I said Saturday or Sunday afternoons was fine but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Here we go. This is the big one, big finale: Is there one thought about your war time experience that you want to share with future generations?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Well, Lord have mercy. One thought? Don't let it happen again I guess is -- I hate of think of what's going to happen now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'm sure that's the answer I'd always get to my question, that's kind of obvious of course.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Yeah, I'd be remiss if it wasn't my answer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's right. Exactly. Can't wait for it to happen again; I don't think so. Do you think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Oh, I think, I think so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, you've been a very good guinea pig, to use the expression. I realized that I don't need to use these questions.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: No. Those are silly.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They are silly. Well, you know, somebody's trying to get general information out of people.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Maybe some people have answers to those things.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: These are good for, there are high school students doing this, so it's good for them to have a list like this.

sp.speaker: Eleanor D. Weil
sp.p: Yeah, they would need it.
